canonicalCards.recommendedFirstExperiment: Move the boundary to a stable consonant, breath, or sustained portion, overlap the takes, and audition a short crossfade.
stopOrUndo: Stop once you can repeatably hear continuous consonant, vowel, ambience, and pitch without a doubled syllable in the full context. Back off or undo if a long crossfade can smear timing or combine two different pitches and rooms.
Return the boundary to its prior position and remove the crossfade.
canonicalCards.teachingPrinciple: Edit boundaries are least audible where waveform, tone, ambience, and articulation are compatible. Silence is not always safest if room tone changes abruptly.

canonicalCards.userIntent: Follow a bounded Logic workflow with a listening target and rollback.

canonicalCards.question: How should I work on double-tracked guitar layers in Logic Pro without making the source or arrangement worse?
canonicalCards.rationale: True double takes create timing and timbral variation that can widen a part. Duplicating one take and shifting it creates different phase and mono behavior.
canonicalCards.recommendedFirstExperiment: Compare two real takes against a duplicated/microshift version at matched level, check mono, and choose the role needed.
stopOrUndo: Stop once you can repeatably hear width and density with stable rhythm and center in the full context. Back off or undo if loose doubles flam; copied/microshift layers comb-filter; too many guitars mask vocals and keys.
Mute support guitar layers and restore pan/timing.

tradeoffs: The session is simpler, but changing one layer now requires rebuilding the print.
Rendering can omit tails, automation, sidechains, or introduce gain changes; later layer revision becomes harder.
A local improvement can create a new timing, tone, noise, phase, density, or arrangement problem.
canonicalCards.userIntent: Adapt to a real tradeoff without restarting from a generic recipe.

contradictions.summary: Edit directly in the Audio File Editor for speed and certainty / Keep all edits region-based or on duplicated files
contradictions.tutorBehavior: Use a short reversible comparison before choosing.
contradictions.whatDecides: Use destructive processing only when the source is archived, the change is approved, and file-wide behavior is intended.

contradictions.summary: Mute every gap for maximum cleanliness / Preserve continuous room tone between phrases
contradictions.tutorBehavior: Use a short reversible comparison before choosing.
contradictions.whatDecides: The noise floor, exposure of the section, number of layers, and audibility of gating determine the better approach.

contradictions.summary: Use a gate or Remove Silence for all cleanup / Edit gaps manually with fades and region gain
contradictions.tutorBehavior: Use a short reversible comparison before choosing.
contradictions.whatDecides: Consistency and volume of the noise favor automation; exposed phrases and irregular material favor manual control.

contradictions.summary: Remove breaths for a polished vocal / Reduce only distracting breaths and preserve phrasing
contradictions.tutorBehavior: Use a short reversible comparison before choosing.
contradictions.whatDecides: Genre, intimacy, compression, stack density, and whether the breath serves the phrase decide.

contradictions.summary: Use automatic breath detection across the whole vocal / Edit breaths manually one by one
contradictions.tutorBehavior: Use a short reversible comparison before choosing.
contradictions.whatDecides: Long consistent sessions favor detection; important exposed vocals and ambiguous consonants favor manual review.

contradictions.summary: A zero crossing guarantees a click-free edit / A short crossfade is still required
contradictions.tutorBehavior: Use a short reversible comparison before choosing.
contradictions.whatDecides: Complex/stereo waveforms, DC offset, and level differences mean zero crossing is only one diagnostic aid.

contradictions.summary: Use the shortest possible crossfade / Use a longer crossfade to blend tone and ambience
contradictions.tutorBehavior: Use a short reversible comparison before choosing.
contradictions.whatDecides: Transient material favors short fades; sustained or room-different material may require longer fades or a different take.

contradictions.summary: Use equal-gain crossfades / Use equal-power crossfades
contradictions.tutorBehavior: Use a short reversible comparison before choosing.
contradictions.whatDecides: Correlation, level, overlap, and the perceived dip or swell decide; audition both at fixed boundaries.

contradictions.summary: Finish the comp before tuning and cleanup / Tune or clean each take before comping
contradictions.tutorBehavior: Use a short reversible comparison before choosing.
contradictions.whatDecides: Comp-first minimizes wasted work; pre-processing may help audition difficult takes but risks bias and duplication.

contradictions.summary: Choose the technically cleanest take / Choose the emotionally strongest take and repair it
contradictions.tutorBehavior: Use a short reversible comparison before choosing.
contradictions.whatDecides: The severity of defects, repair artifacts, and musical role decide; compare in context.

contradictions.summary: Quantize the whole performance / Edit only obvious timing conflicts manually
contradictions.tutorBehavior: Use a short reversible comparison before choosing.
contradictions.whatDecides: Stable grid-based genres favor bounded quantization; rubato, acoustic phrasing, and mixed intentional timing favor manual edits.

contradictions.summary: Make the performance follow the project grid / Make the tempo map follow the performance
contradictions.tutorBehavior: Use a short reversible comparison before choosing.
contradictions.whatDecides: Loop-driven arrangements favor the grid; expressive foundational performances may define tempo.

contradictions.summary: Align doubles tightly / Preserve loose timing for width and humanity
contradictions.tutorBehavior: Use a short reversible comparison before choosing.
contradictions.whatDecides: Lyric intelligibility and rhythmic precision favor tighter onsets; ensemble width and energy favor controlled variation.

contradictions.summary: Align complete vocal phrases / Align consonants but leave vowels less constrained
contradictions.tutorBehavior: Use a short reversible comparison before choosing.
contradictions.whatDecides: Unison pop precision may favor more alignment; natural stacks and harmonies often benefit from protected sustains.

contradictions.summary: Use automatic alignment tools / Manually edit each phrase
contradictions.tutorBehavior: Use a short reversible comparison before choosing.
contradictions.whatDecides: Large consistent stacks favor automation with protected areas; complex phrasing and exposed leads require manual review.

contradictions.summary: Repair timing with Flex Time / Choose another take instead
contradictions.tutorBehavior: Use a short reversible comparison before choosing.
contradictions.whatDecides: Small local timing defects favor Flex; extreme stretch, artifact-prone material, or stronger alternate performances favor comping.

contradictions.summary: Use polyphonic stretching for guitar/piano / Use slicing for transient-rich parts
contradictions.tutorBehavior: Use a short reversible comparison before choosing.
contradictions.whatDecides: Sustained harmonic continuity favors polyphonic methods; isolated attacks with acceptable gaps may favor slicing.

contradictions.summary: Remove bleed from every close microphone / Keep bleed as part of the instrument and room
contradictions.tutorBehavior: Use a short reversible comparison before choosing.
contradictions.whatDecides: Phase coherence, genre, room quality, and exposure determine whether bleed supports or distracts.

contradictions.summary: Time-align room microphones to close mics / Preserve natural room arrival time
contradictions.tutorBehavior: Use a short reversible comparison before choosing.
contradictions.whatDecides: Cancellation problems may justify movement; depth and spatial impression often depend on delay.

contradictions.summary: Remove all audible hiss / Use conservative reduction and accept residual noise
contradictions.tutorBehavior: Use a short reversible comparison before choosing.
contradictions.whatDecides: Exposed speech-like material may tolerate more repair; music, tails, breath, and harmonics often reveal artifacts.

contradictions.summary: Repair every defect in post / Re-record the passage
contradictions.tutorBehavior: Use a short reversible comparison before choosing.
contradictions.whatDecides: Unique performance or unavailable session favors repair; severe artifacts and easy access favor re-recording.

contradictions.summary: Consolidate after every edit phase / Keep live edits until final approval
contradictions.tutorBehavior: Use a short reversible comparison before choosing.
contradictions.whatDecides: CPU/collaboration may favor interim prints, but revision risk favors late consolidation with archived sources.

contradictions.summary: Add layers until the sound is big enough / Replace or redesign the primary source
contradictions.tutorBehavior: Use a short reversible comparison before choosing.
contradictions.whatDecides: A missing specific role may justify a support; broad weakness usually calls for a stronger primary.

contradictions.summary: Keep every layer full and natural / Filter each layer to its assigned role
contradictions.tutorBehavior: Use a short reversible comparison before choosing.
contradictions.whatDecides: Full-range character matters for identity; role filtering is useful only where real overlap exists.

contradictions.summary: Every layer should sound good solo / Support layers may sound incomplete alone
contradictions.tutorBehavior: Use a short reversible comparison before choosing.
contradictions.whatDecides: Standalone reuse favors full tone; a fused composite often needs role-limited supports.

contradictions.summary: Limit every composite to two layers / Use as many layers as the sound requires
contradictions.tutorBehavior: Use a short reversible comparison before choosing.
contradictions.whatDecides: Clarity and efficiency favor few layers; complex cinematic or ensemble designs may justify more when every role is distinct.

contradictions.summary: Sample-align every layer exactly / Align by ear and accept controlled offset
contradictions.tutorBehavior: Use a short reversible comparison before choosing.
contradictions.whatDecides: Related low-frequency samples often need careful timing; ensemble/room layers may benefit from natural spread.

contradictions.summary: Flip polarity before moving samples / Nudge timing before trying polarity
contradictions.tutorBehavior: Use a short reversible comparison before choosing.
contradictions.whatDecides: Polarity is a fast binary test; actual arrival-time differences may require timing, but both should be isolated.

contradictions.summary: Tune all drum layers to the song / Leave transient drum layers untuned
contradictions.tutorBehavior: Use a short reversible comparison before choosing.
contradictions.whatDecides: Sustained/ringing components make tuning relevant; short noise-like transients may not need exact pitch.

contradictions.summary: Use real double performances / Duplicate and microshift one performance
contradictions.tutorBehavior: Use a short reversible comparison before choosing.
contradictions.whatDecides: Real doubles add organic variance; microshift is faster and controlled but carries phase/mono risks.

contradictions.summary: Keep an essential mono/center core / Make every layer wide for maximum size
contradictions.tutorBehavior: Use a short reversible comparison before choosing.
contradictions.whatDecides: Translation and focal stability favor a core; decorative atmospheres can be intentionally fragile.

contradictions.summary: Keep all sub information mono / Preserve natural stereo low-frequency information
contradictions.tutorBehavior: Use a short reversible comparison before choosing.
contradictions.whatDecides: Club/mono translation favors stable sub; real room or stereo instruments may retain some low width if cancellation is controlled.

contradictions.summary: Use EQ to create frequency slots / Change register, voicing, rhythm, and source choice first
contradictions.tutorBehavior: Use a short reversible comparison before choosing.
contradictions.whatDecides: Static overlapping sources may need EQ, but musical allocation often solves masking more naturally.

contradictions.summary: Process all layers on one bus for glue / Process each layer separately before summing
contradictions.tutorBehavior: Use a short reversible comparison before choosing.
contradictions.whatDecides: Shared processing fuses behavior; source-specific conflicts and triggers need individual control.

contradictions.summary: Use Folder Stacks for all layer groups / Use Summing Stacks for layered instruments
contradictions.tutorBehavior: Use a short reversible comparison before choosing.
contradictions.whatDecides: Organization-only needs favor Folder; shared routing/processing and one composite fader favor Summing.

contradictions.summary: Resample layered instruments early / Keep layers editable throughout production
contradictions.tutorBehavior: Use a short reversible comparison before choosing.
contradictions.whatDecides: Creative commitment and CPU favor printing; later arrangement, tuning, and balance revision favor live layers.

contradictions.summary: Keep the layered instrument consistent through the song / Change layers by section
contradictions.tutorBehavior: Use a short reversible comparison before choosing.
contradictions.whatDecides: Continuity favors static identity; contrast and masking control favor section-specific layers.

contradictions.summary: Add a separate attack layer / Shape the original transient
contradictions.tutorBehavior: Use a short reversible comparison before choosing.
contradictions.whatDecides: A missing unique attack timbre favors layering; simple envelope imbalance favors transient shaping.

contradictions.summary: Add a dedicated sub layer / Generate harmonics or redesign one bass source
contradictions.tutorBehavior: Use a short reversible comparison before choosing.
contradictions.whatDecides: Missing fundamental weight favors sub; translation problems often need upper harmonics rather than more sub.

contradictions.summary: Add an ambience recording / Use reverb/delay to create atmosphere
contradictions.tutorBehavior: Use a short reversible comparison before choosing.
contradictions.whatDecides: Specific location and texture favor recorded ambience; coherent controllable space favors effects.

contradictions.summary: Align backing vocals into one pad / Preserve independent ensemble timing
contradictions.tutorBehavior: Use a short reversible comparison before choosing.
contradictions.whatDecides: Modern precise stacks favor tighter onsets; choir-like width and humanity favor controlled differences.

contradictions.summary: Keep breaths in every vocal layer / Keep one lead breath and reduce support breaths
contradictions.tutorBehavior: Use a short reversible comparison before choosing.
contradictions.whatDecides: Natural ensemble realism may retain several; clarity and noise control often favor one anchor.

contradictions.summary: Double the exact guitar part / Use complementary voicings or rhythms
contradictions.tutorBehavior: Use a short reversible comparison before choosing.
contradictions.whatDecides: Wall-of-guitars aesthetics favor doubles; clarity and harmonic detail favor complementary arrangement.

contradictions.summary: Layer piano and synth with the same full voicing / Assign piano transient and synth sustain/register roles
contradictions.tutorBehavior: Use a short reversible comparison before choosing.
contradictions.whatDecides: Dense impact may justify doubling; most mixes benefit from complementary envelope and voicing.

contradictions.summary: Judge each layer by muting in context / Solo each layer to inspect its quality
contradictions.tutorBehavior: Use a short reversible comparison before choosing.
contradictions.whatDecides: Context determines role; solo is still useful for artifacts and source defects but not final contribution.

contradictions.summary: Turn texture up until clearly audible / Keep texture below separate-event perception
contradictions.tutorBehavior: Use a short reversible comparison before choosing.
contradictions.whatDecides: Featured sound design may be obvious; support texture often works best when its absence is noticed.

myths.correction: Complex and stereo waveforms can still jump; DC offset and level changes also matter.
myths.myth: Every click can be fixed by cutting at a zero crossing.

myths.correction: Long overlaps can smear timing, double vowels, and create pitch or phase interaction.
myths.myth: Longer crossfades are always smoother.

myths.correction: Hard silence can reveal edits and make the recording breathe unnaturally.
myths.myth: Silence between phrases is always cleaner than room tone.

myths.correction: Breaths can carry phrasing, realism, and emotional preparation.
myths.myth: Remove every vocal breath for a professional result.

myths.correction: A gate follows detector level and timing, not lyrical or musical meaning.
myths.myth: A noise gate understands musical phrasing.

myths.correction: Aggressive reduction can create watery, metallic, or dull artifacts.
myths.myth: Denoising should make the noise floor completely silent.

myths.correction: Hum often has a base and harmonics, while broad filtering can remove musical fundamentals.
myths.myth: Hum is solved by a broad high-pass filter.

myths.correction: High sensitivity may remove consonants, attacks, or real transients.
myths.myth: De-clicking can safely be run at maximum sensitivity.

myths.correction: Plosives are low-frequency air bursts with different duration and spectrum.
myths.myth: A plosive is just a click.

myths.correction: Waveform display and transient starts do not prove favorable frequency-dependent combination.
myths.myth: If a waveform looks aligned, layered samples are in phase.

myths.correction: Independent edits change inter-mic timing and phase relationships.
myths.myth: Every drum microphone can be edited independently.

myths.correction: Natural delay carries depth and spatial cues.
myths.myth: Room microphones should always be aligned to close microphones.

myths.correction: Full correction can erase phrasing and create stretch artifacts.
myths.myth: Quantizing vocals to 100 percent always sounds professional.

myths.correction: Dense markers create many small stretches and can increase artifacts.
myths.myth: More Flex markers mean more control and better sound.

myths.correction: Expressive performances may define the tempo map.
myths.myth: The grid should always be the timing authority.

myths.correction: Extreme alignment can narrow width and create phasey sameness.
myths.myth: Perfectly aligned doubles are always tighter and wider.

myths.correction: Harmony pitch transitions and phrasing can need different timing.
myths.myth: Every harmony should match lead-vocal timing exactly.

myths.correction: Mechanical noises can support realism and phrasing.
myths.myth: Fret squeaks and pedal noise are always mistakes.

myths.correction: Solo exaggerates details that may be irrelevant in the mix.
myths.myth: Solo is the best place to decide every cleanup edit.

myths.correction: Consolidation changes workflow, not inherent quality, and can omit tails or hide errors.
myths.myth: Consolidating audio improves sound quality.

myths.correction: Alternatives and future revisions may still reference them.
myths.myth: Deleting unused takes is harmless once a comp exists.

myths.correction: Support layers may intentionally supply only attack, body, sub, texture, width, or atmosphere.
myths.myth: Every layer should sound complete by itself.

myths.correction: More layers can increase masking, peaks, and role ambiguity.
myths.myth: More layers always make a sound bigger.

myths.correction: Timing, register, envelope, panning, and hierarchy can allow overlap.
myths.myth: If two layers share frequencies, one must be EQed away.

myths.correction: Musical sources naturally overlap; exclusive slots are neither possible nor always desirable.
myths.myth: Each layer needs a unique frequency slot.

myths.correction: Identity can come from timbre, onset, pitch, or placement, not only level.
myths.myth: The loudest layer is the primary layer.

myths.correction: Texture and atmosphere may work below separate-source perception.
myths.myth: A layer that is not obviously audible is useless.

myths.correction: Overlapping low fundamentals consume headroom and can cancel.
myths.myth: All bass layers should be full range.

myths.correction: Phones need upper harmonics and recognizable articulation, not more inaudible sub.
myths.myth: Adding a sub layer fixes bass translation on phones.

myths.correction: Phase-based width can weaken mono and center stability.
myths.myth: Stereo widening always makes a layered sound larger.

myths.correction: A duplicate is highly correlated and creates comb filtering; real takes contain performance variation.
myths.myth: Duplicating and delaying a track is the same as real double-tracking.

myths.correction: Different layers may need natural offset, and alignment can help one band while hurting another.
myths.myth: Hard-aligning all samples creates maximum punch.

myths.correction: Short noisy transients may not present a stable pitch.
myths.myth: Every drum layer should be tuned exactly to the song key.

myths.correction: Source choice, register, envelope, rhythm, and arrangement often solve the conflict more naturally.
myths.myth: EQ is the first tool for making layers fit.

myths.correction: Solo fullness often duplicates the primary and creates masking.
myths.myth: A support layer should be mixed to sound impressive in solo.

myths.correction: Summing Stacks route members through an aux; Folder Stacks mainly organize/control.
myths.myth: A Summing Stack and Folder Stack are the same except visually.

myths.correction: Shared compression cannot resolve wrong pitch, timing, envelope, or redundant roles.
myths.myth: Bus compression can fix any incoherent layer stack.

myths.correction: It is reversible when the original stack is archived and the render is a new derivative.
myths.myth: Printing a layered instrument is irreversible.

myths.correction: Constant density can reduce section contrast and impact.
myths.myth: Layering the same part through the whole song creates consistency.

myths.correction: The best attack support may only improve definition of the composite.
myths.myth: A transient layer should be clearly audible as a click.

myths.correction: Full-range ambience can mask music and destabilize mono.
myths.myth: An atmosphere layer should fill the entire stereo spectrum.

myths.correction: Equal prominence often blurs lyric and pitch focus.
myths.myth: Vocal doubles should be as loud as the lead for thickness.

myths.correction: Stacked breaths can create a wide noisy rush.
myths.myth: Every backing vocal breath should stay for realism.

myths.correction: Constant full stacks can obscure chord motion and lyric.
myths.myth: Every harmony voice should be present in every chorus line.

myths.correction: Duplicate register and envelope often create mud.
myths.myth: Piano and synth layers should play identical full voicings.

myths.correction: Noise, foley, mechanical, and room textures can add identity without pitch.
myths.myth: Texture must be tonal to layer with an instrument.

myths.correction: Routing does not solve timing, tuning, envelope, or hierarchy.
myths.myth: Layered sounds fuse automatically when routed to one bus.

myths.correction: Arrival-time and filtering relationships are frequency-dependent.
myths.myth: Phase cancellation is always fixed by polarity inversion.

myths.correction: Source separation produces an estimate with artifacts and leakage.
myths.myth: A separated stem is the same as the original isolated layer.

myths.correction: Mechanical detail can communicate touch and realism.
myths.myth: All mechanical noise should be removed from acoustic instruments.

myths.correction: Complex repair may indicate the source or performance should be replaced.
myths.myth: If editing takes a long time, more processing is needed.

myths.correction: Visual smoothness does not prove continuity, timing, or musicality.
myths.myth: An edit is successful if the waveform looks smooth.

myths.correction: Tool uniqueness does not equal perceptual contribution.
myths.myth: A layer is justified because it has a unique plug-in or preset.

myths.correction: Source spectra and arrangements vary by note, time, and performance.
myths.myth: Frequency charts can assign exact bands to every layer.
